stem: A bond is issued at a discount. Over the life of the bond, the carrying amount of the liability and the reported interest expense will, respectively:

options.A: increase and increase.
options.B: increase and decrease.
options.C: decrease and increase.

explanations.A: Correct. Discount amortisation adds to the carrying amount each period, and because interest expense equals the constant market yield times a rising carrying amount, expense rises as well.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Falling interest expense with a rising carrying amount is internally inconsistent under the effective interest method.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A decreasing carrying amount describes a bond issued at a premium.

stem: A company issues a three-year bond with a face value of USD 1,000,000 and a 5% annual coupon when the market yield is 6%. Interest expense in Year 1 under the effective interest method is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 50,000 is the cash coupon; under the effective interest method expense exceeds the coupon for a discount bond.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 60,000 applies the 6% yield to face value rather than to the carrying amount.

stem: A three-year bond with a USD 1,000,000 face value and a 5% annual coupon is issued at USD 973,270 to yield 6%. Its carrying amount at the end of Year 1 is closest to:

explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 973,300 is the original issue price, before any discount amortisation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The carrying amount reaches face value only at maturity.

stem: For a bond issued at a premium, total interest expense recognised over the bond's life is:

options.A: greater than the total coupon payments.
options.B: less than the total coupon payments.
options.C: equal to the total coupon payments.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Expense exceeding coupons is the discount case.
explanations.B: Correct. The premium received at issuance is amortised as a reduction of interest expense, so cumulative expense equals total coupons less the premium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Equality holds only for a bond issued exactly at par.

stem: Under IFRS 16, a lessee accounts for essentially all leases by:

options.A: recognising a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet.
options.B: disclosing the future minimum payments in the notes only.
options.C: classifying the lease as either operating or finance, with operating leases kept off balance sheet.

explanations.A: Correct. IFRS 16 uses a single lessee model: an ROU asset and lease liability are recognised (with short-term and low-value exemptions), producing amortisation plus interest rather than rent expense.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Note-only disclosure is the superseded pre-IFRS 16 operating-lease treatment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. US GAAP retains the operating/finance distinction for expense presentation, but even US GAAP operating leases are now on balance sheet.

stem: Compared with a US GAAP operating lease, a finance lease of the same asset will most likely report:

options.A: higher cash flow from operations and higher total expense in the early years.
options.B: lower cash flow from operations and lower total expense in the early years.
options.C: identical cash flow from operations and identical expense in every year.

explanations.A: Correct. Under a finance lease the principal portion of the payment is a financing outflow, so CFO is higher; interest plus amortisation exceeds the straight-line operating lease expense in the early years.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both effects run the other way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Total cash flow is identical, but its classification and the expense profile differ.

stem: The net pension liability reported on the balance sheet for a defined benefit plan is:

options.A: the projected benefit obligation less the fair value of plan assets.
options.B: the accumulated benefit obligation less contributions made during the year.
options.C: the total of contractual future benefit payments.

explanations.A: Correct. The funded status — the defined benefit obligation net of plan assets at fair value — is recognised directly on the balance sheet under both IFRS and US GAAP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Contributions affect plan assets but are not netted against the obligation in this way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Undiscounted future payments overstate the obligation; the obligation is a present value.

stem: Under IFRS, actuarial gains and losses on a defined benefit pension plan (remeasurements) are:

options.A: recognised in profit or loss immediately.
options.B: recognised in other comprehensive income and not subsequently reclassified to profit or loss.
options.C: amortised into profit or loss using the corridor approach.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Only service cost and net interest on the net liability go through profit or loss under IAS 19.
explanations.B: Correct. Remeasurements go to OCI and stay there; they are never recycled through profit or loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The corridor approach was eliminated from IAS 19; a form of deferred amortisation survives only under US GAAP.

stem: An increase in the discount rate used to measure a defined benefit obligation will most likely:

options.A: increase the obligation and increase the net pension liability.
options.B: decrease the obligation and decrease the net pension liability.
options.C: leave the obligation unchanged but increase service cost.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A higher discount rate reduces, not increases, the present value of future benefits.
explanations.B: Correct. The obligation is a present value, so raising the discount rate lowers it and improves funded status — a common lever for flattering reported pension figures.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both the obligation and current service cost fall when the discount rate rises.

stem: A debt covenant requiring the company to maintain a minimum interest coverage ratio is best described as:

options.A: an affirmative covenant.
options.B: a negative covenant.
options.C: a subordination clause.

explanations.A: Correct. Affirmative covenants require the borrower to do something — maintain ratios, provide statements, keep insurance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Negative covenants restrict actions, such as prohibiting additional debt or asset sales.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Subordination governs claim priority in liquidation, not ongoing financial performance.

stem: On the quality spectrum, financial reports that are GAAP-compliant but reflect biased choices within the standards are best described as:

options.A: high quality and decision useful.
options.B: lower quality, because the reporting is compliant but not neutral.
options.C: fraudulent.

explanations.A: Incorrect. High-quality reporting requires both compliance and decision-useful, unbiased content.
explanations.B: Correct. Compliance is a floor, not a guarantee; biased estimates and aggressive-but-permissible choices sit between high quality and outright non-compliance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fraud involves fictitious transactions or deliberate non-compliance, which is further along the spectrum.

stem: Receivables growing substantially faster than revenue, combined with a rising gap between net income and cash flow from operations, most likely signals:

options.A: conservative revenue recognition.
options.B: aggressive revenue recognition or channel stuffing.
options.C: an improvement in working capital management.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Conservative recognition would delay revenue and tend to shrink, not inflate, receivables relative to sales.
explanations.B: Correct. Revenue booked without corresponding collections builds receivables and widens the accrual gap — the classic signature of premature recognition or loading the distribution channel.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Better working capital management would shorten, not lengthen, the collection cycle.

stem: The three conditions commonly present when low-quality financial reporting occurs are:

options.A: motivation, opportunity, and rationalisation.
options.B: materiality, measurement, and disclosure.
options.C: leverage, liquidity, and profitability.

explanations.A: Correct. Pressure or incentive to misreport, weak controls or vague standards that create the opportunity, and a self-justifying rationalisation together form the classic fraud triangle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. These are accounting concepts, not behavioural conditions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. These are financial characteristics that may create motivation but do not describe the full set of conditions.

stem: A company reclassifies a recurring operating expense as a non-recurring restructuring charge. This is best described as:

options.A: a classification shift that inflates recurring operating earnings.
options.B: a change in accounting estimate applied prospectively.
options.C: a permanent difference affecting the effective tax rate.

explanations.A: Correct. Total net income is unchanged, but the earnings base analysts extrapolate is flattered — one of the most common and hardest-to-detect quality issues.
explanations.B: Incorrect. No estimate has changed; only the label on the expense has.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tax treatment is unaffected by presentation within pre-tax income.

stem: Which of the following would an analyst most likely view as a sign of conservative, high-quality accounting?

options.A: Lengthening the depreciable lives of core production assets.
options.B: Recognising a warranty provision that has consistently proven adequate relative to actual claims.
options.C: Capitalising a growing share of software development costs.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Longer lives reduce depreciation and inflate current earnings, an aggressive choice absent supporting evidence.
explanations.B: Correct. Provisions that track actual outcomes indicate disciplined, unbiased estimation rather than a cookie-jar reserve or systematic understatement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A rising capitalisation rate defers costs and is an aggressive choice that requires scrutiny.

stem: The Beneish M-score is best described as a model that:

options.A: estimates the probability that a company has manipulated its earnings.
options.B: predicts the probability of bankruptcy within two years.
options.C: measures the sustainable growth rate of a company.

explanations.A: Correct. The M-score combines eight variables — including days sales in receivables, gross margin, asset quality, and total accruals — into a probit-style manipulation score.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bankruptcy prediction is the purpose of the Altman Z-score.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sustainable growth is retention ratio times ROE, unrelated to the M-score.

stem: In assessing the credit quality of a corporate borrower, an analyst would place the greatest weight on:

options.A: earnings per share growth.
options.B: leverage and cash-flow-based coverage of fixed obligations.
options.C: the price-to-book ratio.

explanations.A: Incorrect. EPS is an equity-holder metric distorted by share count and does not measure debt service capacity.
explanations.B: Correct. Credit analysis centres on scale, leverage, and whether recurring cash flow reliably covers interest and maturities across a cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Price-to-book is a market-based valuation multiple, not a measure of repayment capacity.

stem: Before comparing two companies that use different inventory cost formulas, an analyst should:

options.A: restate the LIFO reporter's inventory and cost of goods sold onto a FIFO basis.
options.B: ignore the difference, since it affects only the balance sheet.
options.C: convert both companies' statements to a cash basis.

explanations.A: Correct. The LIFO reserve disclosure allows a like-for-like restatement of inventory, COGS, equity, and the associated deferred tax, which is the standard comparability adjustment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The choice affects COGS, gross margin, net income, and taxes as well as inventory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Discarding accruals entirely destroys the very measures being compared.

stem: When using screening ratios to build an equity portfolio, a key limitation an analyst must address is that:

options.A: ratios are not comparable across companies using different accounting policies.
options.B: ratios cannot be computed from audited financial statements.
options.C: ratios are always forward looking.

explanations.A: Correct. Differences in cost formulas, capitalisation policy, depreciation methods, and reporting frameworks make unadjusted ratios non-comparable, which is why screens need normalisation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Audited statements are the standard input for ratio computation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ratios computed from reported statements are backward looking; forecasting them is a separate step.

stem: An analyst adjusting reported financial statements to forecast future performance should most appropriately:

options.A: remove items identified as non-recurring and reassess the sustainability of the remaining earnings base.
options.B: use reported net income unadjusted, because it is audited.
options.C: exclude all non-cash charges, including depreciation, from the forecast.

explanations.A: Correct. Forecasting requires isolating the recurring, repeatable component of earnings and cash flow, which means scrutinising restructuring charges, gains on disposal, and one-off tax items.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Audit assurance concerns fair presentation, not persistence of the reported figures.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Depreciation proxies for the consumption of capacity and cannot simply be discarded from a going-concern forecast.
